setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. You and three coworkers have two weeks to update {document|the} for the whole team.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are one of four people assigned to update {document|the} together.
pressure: {coworker3} says it will be faster if everyone just starts on something.
The first week is almost over.
detail: The project has its own shared folder.

tiers.1: A team cannot work toward a goal it has not defined.
tiers.2: Clear roles prevent wasted and missing work.
tiers.3: Duplicate work should be sorted out as soon as it is found.
tiers.4: A teammate falling behind needs a supportive check-in.
tiers.5: Recognizing contributions keeps a team motivated.

fact: The team is not sure what the finished {document} needs to include.
clear: {Lead|the} gave the team a written list of what the finished {document} must include.
issues.done: the team already has a written list of requirements
issues.action: Suggest asking {lead|the} for a clear list of what the finished work must include.
issues.brief: ask {lead|the} what the finished work must include
issues.reason: A team that is unsure of the goal may build the wrong thing. A clear list keeps everyone aimed at the same result.
issues.lesson: Make sure the team agrees on the goal before dividing up the work.

shortcut.text: Let each person decide what the {document} should include.
shortcut.why: Four separate ideas of the goal produce work that does not fit together.
shortcut.mis: Everyone will naturally aim for the same result.

fact: Nobody has agreed who is doing which part.
clear: The team already wrote down who is doing each part.
issues.action: Suggest the team agree on who does each part and write it down.
issues.brief: agree on and write down roles
issues.reason: Without agreed roles, some parts get done twice and others not at all.
issues.lesson: Agree on roles and write them down so every part has an owner.

shortcut.text: Start on whichever part looks most interesting to you.
shortcut.brief: start on the most interesting part
shortcut.why: Picking your favorite part without agreement risks duplicate or missing work.
shortcut.mis: Interest is a good way to split up work.

fact: You discover that {coworker} has been working on the same section as you.
issues.action: Tell {coworker} right away and agree on who keeps that section.
issues.brief: agree with {coworker} on who keeps it
issues.reason: Duplicate work wastes effort. Sorting it out quickly frees one of you for another part.
issues.lesson: Raise overlapping work right away so the team can rebalance.

shortcut.text: Keep going so your version is the better one.
shortcut.why: Competing on the same section wastes both people's time and creates friction.
shortcut.mis: Competition produces the best work on a team.

fact: {coworker2} has not started a part that two other people are waiting on.
issues.action: Check in with {coworker2} privately to ask how it is going and whether help is needed.
issues.brief: check in with {coworker2} and offer help
issues.reason: {coworker2} may be stuck or overloaded. A supportive check-in solves the problem without blame.
issues.lesson: When a teammate is behind, check in and offer help before assuming the worst.

shortcut.text: Complain to the rest of the team that {coworker2} is slowing everyone down.
shortcut.why: Complaining behind someone's back damages trust and does not get the part started.
shortcut.mis: Pointing out a slow teammate fixes the delay.

fact: {coworker3}'s suggestion is what made the plan work, but nobody has said so.
issues.action: Point out {coworker3}'s contribution when the team next meets.
issues.reason: Recognizing contributions shows respect and encourages people to keep offering ideas.

shortcut.text: Leave it unsaid, since good ideas are just part of the job.
shortcut.why: Unrecognized contributions discourage people from sharing ideas.
shortcut.mis: Recognition is unnecessary on a team.

proceed.text: Keep working on your part and share progress at the next team meeting.
proceed.why: The goal and roles are clear, so steady work on your part and regular updates are what the team needs.
proceed.lesson: Once goals and roles are clear, do your part and keep the team informed.

generic.text: Do the whole project yourself to make sure it is done right.
generic.why: Taking over shuts teammates out and is not sustainable.
generic.mis: The best way to ensure quality is to do it all yourself.

generic.text: Wait for {lead|the} to notice any problems with the team.
generic.why: Team members share responsibility for raising problems.
generic.mis: Only a supervisor should deal with team problems.

overcaution.text: Call an extra meeting to review the roles again.
overcaution.why: The roles are already written down. Another meeting takes time from the work.
overcaution.mis: More meetings make a team work better.

setup: You are part of a four-person team at {workplace|the} updating {document|the}.

goal: The team is unsure what the finished work should contain.
behind: One part that others depend on has not been started.

steps.text: Get a clear list of requirements from {lead|the}
Agree on who does each part
Check in with anyone who is stuck
Combine the parts and review them together

rel: You divide work once you know what the whole needs.
Everyone needs a role before starting.
Check-ins happen while the work is in progress.
Every part has to be done before combining.
Parts are combined after they are done.
process.lesson: Define the goal, assign roles, support each other through the work, then combine.

title: Team chat: {document} project
intro: You are reviewing the team's planning chat before the next meeting.
doc.lesson: Good team communication sets clear roles and deadlines, and treats everyone's work with respect.

lines.text: {coworker}: Here is the list from {lead|the} of what the {document} must include.
lines.fine: Shares the goal with the team.

lines.text: {coworker2}: I will take sections 1 and 2; you take 3, and {coworker3} takes 4.
lines.fine: Clear roles with an owner for each section.

bad.text: {coworker2}: Let us all just work on whatever and see how it turns out.
bad.why: Without roles, work gets duplicated or missed.

lines.text: {coworker3}: Drafts due Thursday so we have Friday to combine.
lines.fine: A shared deadline with time to combine.

lines.text: {coworker}: If anyone gets stuck, post here and someone will help.
lines.fine: Invites people to ask for help.

bad.text: {coworker}: If you get stuck, figure it out yourself.
bad.why: Discouraging requests for help leaves teammates stuck and slows the team.

lines.text: {coworker2}: Section 4 is solid; one table could use a heading.

bad.text: {coworker2}: Section 4 is useless, so I am rewriting it myself.
bad.why: Dismissing a teammate's work and taking it over is disrespectful and damages the team.

lines.text: {coworker3}: I will have section 4 done by Thursday as planned.

bad.text: {coworker3}: I will start section 4 sometime next week.
bad.why: Drafts are due Thursday. Starting next week breaks the team's plan without discussing it.

kits.familyName: Covering when the team is short-staffed
setup: You work as {role|a} at {workplace|a}. A coworker called out sick, and the team is covering the extra work.
As {role|a} at {workplace|a}, you are working a shift where the team is one person short.
pressure: {coworker3} says everyone should just look after their own work today.
It is a busier day than usual.
detail: The absent coworker usually works the morning shift.

tiers.1: A task that needs two people for safety cannot be done alone.
tiers.2: Work that nobody owns needs an owner right away.
tiers.3: You need to know where the work stands before picking it up.
tiers.4: Frustration about staffing is best channeled toward a fix.
tiers.5: Thanking teammates matters once the work is covered.

fact: A task the posted procedure says needs two people is due, and only you are free.
issues.action: Hold off on the two-person task until someone can help, and tell {lead|the}.
issues.brief: wait for a second person and tell {lead|the}
issues.reason: The procedure requires two people for safety. Telling the lead lets them find a second person.
issues.lesson: Never do a two-person task alone to cover a gap; get help instead.

shortcut.text: Do the two-person task alone, carefully, since everyone else is busy.
shortcut.why: Being careful does not replace the second person the procedure requires.
shortcut.mis: Being short-staffed justifies skipping safety rules.

fact: Nobody has picked up {task|the}, which the absent coworker usually does.
issues.action: Offer to take {task|the} and tell the team so nobody doubles up.
issues.brief: take on the task and tell the team
issues.reason: Shared responsibility means someone steps up. Telling the team prevents two people doing it.
issues.lesson: When work is left uncovered, offer to own it and tell the team.

shortcut.text: Assume someone else will notice it and pick it up.
shortcut.brief: assume someone else will do it
shortcut.why: When everyone assumes someone else will do it, nobody does.
shortcut.mis: Uncovered work will get picked up by someone.

fact: You do not know where the absent coworker left off on an open order.
clear: The absent coworker left detailed handoff notes on the open order.
issues.done: the handoff notes already explain where things stand
issues.short: not knowing where the order stands
issues.action: Check the handoff log or ask {lead|the} where the order stands.
issues.reason: Starting without knowing the status risks redoing or skipping steps.
issues.lesson: Find out where shared work stands before you pick it up.

shortcut.text: Start the order over from the beginning to be safe.
shortcut.why: Restarting may duplicate finished steps and waste materials.
shortcut.mis: Starting over is always the safe choice.

fact: {coworker2} complains loudly that the team always gets stuck covering.
issues.action: Acknowledge the frustration and suggest raising staffing with {lead|the} later.
issues.brief: acknowledge it and suggest raising it later
issues.reason: The frustration may be fair. Pointing it toward a real conversation helps more than arguing or piling on.
issues.lesson: Respond to team frustration by acknowledging it and steering toward a fix.

shortcut.text: Join in the complaining so {coworker2} knows you agree.
shortcut.why: Piling on lowers morale and does not change staffing.
shortcut.mis: Agreeing with complaints builds team spirit.

fact: {coworker3} stayed late yesterday so the team could finish.
issues.action: Thank {coworker3} for staying late to help the team.
issues.reason: Thanking teammates for extra effort shows respect and keeps people willing to help.
issues.lesson: Notice and thank teammates who go beyond their share.

shortcut.text: Say nothing, since covering is just part of the job.
shortcut.why: Unacknowledged extra effort can leave teammates feeling taken for granted.
shortcut.mis: Thanks are unnecessary for expected work.

proceed.text: Pitch in on the shared work and keep the team updated on what you are covering.
proceed.why: The work is covered and nothing else needs handling, so pitching in and communicating is the teamwork the day needs.
proceed.lesson: On short-staffed days, pitch in and keep everyone informed.

generic.text: Do only your usual tasks, since the extra work is not your job.
generic.why: Team members share responsibility when someone is out.
generic.mis: You are only responsible for your own tasks.

generic.text: Take a long break, since the day is already behind.
generic.why: Disappearing on a short-staffed day puts more on everyone else.
generic.mis: If the day is behind anyway, a long break does not matter.

overcaution.text: Ask {lead|the} to assign every single task before you do anything.
overcaution.why: The work is already covered. Waiting for full assignments wastes time.
overcaution.mis: Nothing should be done without a supervisor's assignment.

setup: Your team at {workplace|the} is one person short today.

dropped: One of the absent coworker's tasks has no owner today.
handoff: The absent coworker's open order is partly done.

steps.text: Meet briefly with the team to split up the work
Find out where the open order stands
Update the team at the end of the shift

rel: Claiming happens as the team splits the work.
You claim the task before working on it.
You need the status before continuing the order.
The team splits work before starting.
The update reports what was done.
process.lesson: Split the work, claim what is uncovered, find where things stand, then update the team.

review.notes: Two-person requirement stated as a posted procedure.
